newsitem.title: USA: New York lawmakers preserve rent laws for six years.
newsitem.headline: New York lawmakers preserve rent laws for six years.

text.p: New York state lawmakers ended a drawn-out battle Monday by hammering out an 11th-hour deal largely preserving laws that hold down rents for millions of tenants.

Republican Gov. George Pataki and legislative leaders worked out a tentative agreement in Albany that keeps the laws mostly intact for another six years. The deal was reached shortly after the decades-old rules technically expired at midnight Sunday.
The rules govern 1.2 million apartments and affect 2.7 million state residents, mostly in New York City. The state legislature is expected to vote on the accord early this week.
"This is a victory for New Yorkers and I think that the vast majority of people will agree with that," Pataki said. "... The extremists on both sides are going to be unhappy."

Pataki, who brokered the accord in 14 hours of talks between Democratic and Republican leaders, also said the deal would protect tenants and would help spur market competition and the construction of new housing.
Lou Rudin, head of a landlords' watchdog committee on abuse of tenants, said he was pleased with the accord even though it limited how much landlords could raise rents.
"We're delighted that a resolution was made and our prediction that the bomb (would) not go off at 12:01 was correct," he said.

The issue of what to do about the expiring restrictions on rent has entangled New York lawmakers for months. It also riveted New York City, where residents pore over obituaries for tipoffs on newly vacant regulated apartments, and one of the most popular Broadway musicals, "Rent," concerns how struggling artists pay for housing.
The rent laws were first put in place during World War II as an emergency measure to control what landlords can charge tenants. The rules were intended to protect low- and middle-income renters.

But critics charged that the laws distorted the market by creating sharp disparities between rents charged in the same building. They also said the rules hampered construction of new housing and cost New York City at least $100 million a year in property tax revenues.

The centerpiece of the tentative deal is an agreement that would grant landlords a 20-percent rent increase on an empty apartment if the former tenant lived there at least eight years. The previous rule allowed rent hikes of between 14 and 16 percent on empty units.
An additional $100-a-month bonus would be allowed on vacant apartments that had rents of $300 a month or less for eight years or more.

The accord also removes rent protections for tenants with high annual incomes. It lowers the threshold from $250,000 a year to $175,000, and the income limits apply to apartments renting for at least $2,000 a month.

Although New York's three major newspapers backed reform, most New Yorkers balked at changes. A New York Times poll last week showed 70 percent of New York's eight million residents believed regulations were needed to provide affordable housing and to keep rents from rising.

The fight over rent regulation involved a face-off between state Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno, an upstate Republican who backed letting all rent rules expire, and Democratic Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver of Manhattan, an advocate of keeping them unchanged.
